newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU anti-dumping policy not favouritism - Brittan.
newsitem.headline: EU anti-dumping policy not favouritism - Brittan.

text.p: European Union anti-dumping policies do not target specific countries or groups of countries, Sir Leon Brittan, the European Commissioner with responsiblity for trade, told a seminar on Monday.
"When it is applied there is no question that we are conducting some sort of industrial policy," Brittan told a conference on EU anti-dumping policy and Central and Eastern European Countries.
"In general, imports from Eastern Europe do not cause the EU many problems and ... the impact of anti-dumping on our trade relationship is minimal."
Brittan said the EU's anti-dumping policies were always going to be a source of complaint from some sections of the market.
"Those of you from Central and Eastern Europe may feel that the application of anti-dumping has penalised your export performance ... or held back your transition to the market," he said.
"On the other hand, there may be some here from European Union industry who feel strongly that unfairly priced imports have taken (their) market share."
Brittan said such differences were "never helpful to the cause of a smooth trading relationship ... nor do they reflect reality."

The conference, organised by the European Commission -- the EU's executive -- aims to explain what often appears to be a byzantine anti-dumping policy that mystifies and frequently angers the 15-nation bloc's trade partners.

Commission officials privately admit that the complexity of anti-dumping legislation -- as summed up by a case published in the Official Journal on Monday -- is often perceived by EU trading partners as aimed at cutting their competitive edges.
In Monday's case, the EU announced it was imposing stiff anti-dumping duties on Malaysian and Chinese manufacturers of steel ring-binder mechanisms used in files for keeping paper.

Asian trade experts told Reuters that non-EU manufacturers were perplexed by how such an obscure product could attract a year-long study resulting in a 30-page document that detailed the differences between ring-binders with varied numbers of metal hoops.

"All of this work for what is a very small market," said one diplomat. "Someone finds a market where they can produce goods cheaply and sell them at a profit and the next thing you know the door is slammed shut. Is that fair?"
In his speech to the seminar, Brittan stressed that the EU levied fewest anti-dumping tariffs against countries with open markets.

"Markets which are very open will be subject to tough competition," he said. "This competition will in turn keep down domestic price levels and make it very difficult for any firm to earn the sort of excess profits in their home markets which would enable them to afford to dump abroad."
Having seen a copy of Brittan's speech, one trade lobbyist scoffed: "This suggests Chinese manufacturers are selling their ring-binder files at enormous profit back home. Pull the other one!".

Brittan said that while the EU "cannot and should not" apply anti-dumping policy in a political way, efforts were being made to offer East and Central European countries special help by opening up the complaints sytem to wider scrutiny.
"This combination of early warning and more direct involvement has undoubtedly helped defuse some of the sensitivity surrounding anti-dumping," he said.

Brittan said the EU was considering ways in which, rather than impose anti-dumping duties on East and Central European products, manufacturers themselves would be given the opportunity to get their house in order.

"This flexibility cannot of course be unconditional," he said. "The firms themselves must be able to show they are not targeting any individual market. If they breach these conditions the undertakings would have to be withdrawn."
